name: SiTime
short_description: Replaces quartz resonators with MEMS-based clocks, oscillators and timing chips.
why_relevant: The silicon clock company now shipping timing in most modern electronics.
history: Founded in 2004 by MEMS veterans, SiTime set out to replace quartz resonators with silicon timing built on MEMS technology, shipping its first oscillators within two years. The company scaled across consumer, automotive, aerospace and defense markets, surpassing one billion units shipped, and acquired Aura Semiconductor in 2022 to broaden its oscillator and real-time-clock portfolio. Publicly traded and headquartered in Silicon Valley, SiTime now counts most leading electronics OEMs among its customers, positioning silicon timing as the new standard.

name: Tenstorrent
short_description: Builds AI RISC-V chips and legendary hardware decks with Jim Keller.
why_relevant: Independent AI silicon plus open software stack taking on NVIDIA.
history: Founded in 2016 by Ljubisa Bajic, Tenstorrent designed AI accelerators around high-bandwidth on-chip mesh interconnect, launching Grayskull and Wormhole silicon and building an open-source software stack. In 2021 the company hired legendary CPU architect Jim Keller as CTO, pivoting toward integrated RISC-V CPU-plus-accelerator platforms. With funding from major venture and strategic investors, Tenstorrent signed licensing partnerships across Asia and Europe and now positions itself as the leading open alternative in AI silicon.

name: Rivos
short_description: Designs RISC-V server chips with matrix engines for AI workloads.
why_relevant: Strongly funded attempt at open-ISA AI servers.
history: Rivos was founded in 2021 by silicon veterans Brian Zimmer and Ranga Venkatesh, both formerly of Google, to develop RISC-V server processors with AI-focused data-parallel vector units. The company raised a $250M Series A in 2023 and has since been scaling its team and tape-outs, publicly demonstrating its processor roadmap toward open-ISA AI servers. Still in its growth phase, Rivos remains one of the strongest-funded attempts to bring open architecture to data-center AI.

name: Ampere Computing
short_description: ARM64 cloud processors built for energy-efficient hyperscale compute.
why_relevant: Gave cloud the efficient ARM alternative to Intel-era servers.
history: Ampere Computing was founded in 2017 by Renee James, former president of Intel, to build power-efficient ARM64 cloud processors for today's hyperscale data centers. The company shipped its 80-core Altra chip in 2021 and the custom-core AmpereOne family in 2023, with Oracle and other cloud providers adopting its platforms. Backed by Oracle and Carlyle among others, Ampere continues to expand its single-socket server line targeting general-purpose compute and AI acceleration.

name: Axelera AI
short_description: European in-memory compute accelerator for edge inference.
why_relevant: EU autonomy in edge-AI chips with 20x power efficiency.
history: Axelera AI was founded in 2021 in Eindhoven to build European edge-AI accelerators based on digital in-memory computing. The company raised a €38M Series A in 2023, followed by a $59M Series B led by Invest-NL in 2025, advancing its Metis platform and preparing its first chip for launch. It now works with European system integrators on industrial, smart-city and security deployments, marketed around roughly 20x power-efficiency gains.

name: Untether AI
short_description: Memory-near compute chip that eliminates expensive data movement.
why_relevant: Runs inference with compute under the SRAM, not next to it.
history: Untether AI was founded in 2018 in Toronto to place compute directly beneath memory, eliminating data movement in AI inference. The company raised C$200M in 2021 and commercialized its runAI acceleration cards built on tsunAImi memory-near processing. With support from Canada's federal and provincial governments alongside strategic investors, it continues to target edge and data-center inference, focusing on memory bandwidth rather than compute-centric architectures.

name: d-Matrix
short_description: In-memory compute designed specifically for generative transformer workloads.
why_relevant: Pushes token economics by computing inside the memory arrays.
history: Founded in 2019 by Sid Sheth, d-Matrix builds in-memory computing chiplets designed for generative transformer workloads, anchored on its Corsair inference architecture. The company secured a $110M Series B in 2023 and announced a $180M raise in 2025 to scale production, with early platforms running generative AI inference for customers. It remains focused on improving token economics by computing inside memory arrays rather than moving data.

name: Eliyan
short_description: Semiconductor IP that links chiplets at maximum bandwidth without silicon interposers.
why_relevant: Removes the interposer cost holding back chiplet-scale computing.
history: Eliyan was founded in 2021 by veteran interconnect designer Ramin Farjadrad to remove the silicon interposer from chiplet-scale designs. The company unveiled its NuLink PHY targeting multi-tera-bit bandwidth, closed a $60M Series B in 2021, and continued licensing its UCIe and PCIe physical layers to major semiconductor partners. As AI chips scale past the limits of monolithic packaging, Eliyan positions its IP as the low-cost bridge for bandwidth-hungry chiplets.

name: Celestial AI
short_description: Photonic fabric moves data chip-to-chip at the speed of light inside the box.
why_relevant: A serious candidate to end the data-movement bottleneck for accelerators.
history: Celestial AI was founded in 2020 by entrepreneur David Lazovsky and MIT professor Rajeev Ram to build a photonic memory fabric for AI accelerators. The company raised a $100M Series B in 2023 and a $250M Series C in 2024, advancing its Photonic Fabric platform and partnering with data-center and semiconductor firms. It aims to end the electrical data-movement bottleneck, moving large memory bases at the speed of light.

name: Lightmatter
short_description: Optical interconnects and computing for deep learning data movement.
why_relevant: Rethinks compute boundaries with optics instead of copper.
history: Lightmatter was founded in 2017 by MIT researchers Nick Harris and Darius Bunandar to bring photonic computing and interconnects to deep learning. The company shipped its Passage optical interconnect, raised a $154M Series B in 2021, and closed a $400M-plus round in 2024 to grow manufacturing capacity for data-center photonics. It now supplies optical switch fabrics and interconnects to customers building next-generation AI systems.

name: Ayar Labs
short_description: Replaces copper with photonic I/O to unlock AI rack-scale memory.
why_relevant: Gives chiplets the PHY to scale clusters beyond power limits.
history: Ayar Labs, spun out of university research and co-founded in 2015 by MIT alumnus Chen Sun, develops in-package optical I/O that replaces copper links in AI systems. The company raised $130M in 2023 with HPE among its backers and announced TeraPHY optical I/O modules delivering multi-terabit links. It continues validating its technology with major silicon and systems partners, pushing rack-scale memory and power-scalable AI clusters.

name: Syntiant
short_description: Ultra-low-power chips that run neural networks on a fraction of a milliwatt.
why_relevant: Always-on audio AI in earbuds that never need charging fear.
history: Syntiant was founded in 2017 to build ultra-low-power analog neural-network accelerators for always-on audio AI. The company raised $55M in 2021 with backers including Microsoft, and its NDP chips have shipped in tens of millions of consumer earbuds and IoT sensors. It has since expanded into edge vision and on-device generative AI with automotive partners, sustaining its leadership in sub-milliwatt inference.

name: Ventana Micro
short_description: High-performance RISC-V CPU running the biggest open architecture servers.
why_relevant: Shipped RISC-V capable of serious cloud workloads.
history: Ventana Micro was founded in 2018 by former SiFive leaders to build high-performance RISC-V server CPUs. The company announced its Veyron V1 core in 2021 as one of the fastest open-ISA designs at the time, landed a $100M funding round in 2022, and signed licensing agreements spanning edge to data-center silicon. It has expanded partnerships with cloud and automotive customers while pushing RISC-V toward serious hyperscale workloads.

name: Efinix
short_description: Efficient programmable logic with built-in RISC-V hosts for edge systems.
why_relevant: Made programmable chips cheap enough for consumer robotics.
history: Efinix was founded in 2012 to reinvent programmable logic with its Quantum fabric, a four-input-LUT architecture that cuts the cost and power of FPGA technology. The company shipped its Trion family, followed by Titanium FPGAs with embedded RISC-V hosts, and raised $26M in 2022 from investors including Samsung. Its low-cost programmable chips have found homes in consumer robotics, edge AI and hardware acceleration.

name: Atomera
short_description: Mears silicon technology boosts transistor performance of legacy fabs.
why_relevant: Upgrade path for older fabs to stay relevant for years.
history: Atomera was founded in 2007 to commercialize Mears Silicon Technology (MST), a dopant-engineered ultra-thin film that improves transistor performance in existing fabs. The company listed on Nasdaq in 2016 and has since signed multiple technology license agreements with semiconductor manufacturers across foundry nodes. It continues to pitch a lower-risk upgrade path for older and current fabs targeting performance gains without full redesign.

name: Nantero
short_description: NRAM memory built from carbon nanotubes for durability and speed.
why_relevant: Non-volatile memory that survives radiation and heat better than flash.
history: Nantero was founded in 2001, rooted in research at Harvard University, to develop NRAM, a carbon-nanotube non-volatile memory offering strong endurance, heat and radiation tolerance. The company achieved joint-development milestones with Fujitsu and raised a $200M round in 2017 to build its first US fab. It continues licensing NRAM for embedded, industrial and high-reliability applications where flash falls short, working with memory partners on qualification.

name: Weebit Nano
short_description: Resistive RAM licensed into fabs for embedded memory swaps.
why_relevant: Drops into existing CMOS with 100x faster writes than flash.
history: Weebit Nano was incorporated in 2015 to develop silicon-oxide RRAM and pursued an ASX listing in Australia, reaching the public market in 2021. The company qualified its embedded RRAM with SkyWater and signed further licensing and supply agreements with fabs in the following years. It remains a publicly traded IP provider pushing a drop-in, 100x-faster-write alternative to flash in embedded memory applications.

name: FuriosaAI
short_description: Korean AI chip startup shipping the RNGD accelerator.
why_relevant: Samsung-fabricated silicon with a serious software stack.
history: FuriosaAI was founded in 2017 by researchers tied to Seoul National University to build AI accelerators for deep learning. The company shipped its second-generation RNGD accelerator, produced at Samsung's foundry, backed by substantial Korean funding across multiple rounds. It continues developing LLM-focused accelerators and a serious software stack for data-center deployment in Korea and Japan.

name: Rebellions
short_description: AI chip startup behind the ATOM NPU for consumer devices.
why_relevant: Merged with Sapeon to form Korea's national AI chip champion.
history: Rebellions was founded in 2020 to build AI chips for on-device and data-center workloads, launching the ATOM NPU for consumer devices. The startup raised a $100M-plus Series A and developed the REBEL data-center accelerator through Samsung's foundry in Korea. In 2024 it agreed to merge with Sapeon, forming a combined national AI-chip champion targeting transformer-optimized NPUs for cloud and edge.

name: Sapeon
short_description: SK-affiliated developer of data-center AI accelerators, merging with Rebellions.
why_relevant: Part of Korea's fast-track national AI semiconductor consolidation.
history: Sapeon was spun out of SK Telecom in 2022 to develop data-center AI accelerators, delivering its X330 NPU with Samsung's foundry. The company worked within the SK Group ecosystem toward a national AI-silicon agenda and agreed in 2024 to merge with Rebellions. That consolidation creates Korea's leading domestic supplier of data-center NPUs, combining SK Telecom's capital and channels with Rebellions' engineering talent.

name: Kneron
short_description: Tiny on-device AI for IoT devices with 'AI-in-sensor' architecture.
why_relevant: Brings smart vision to low-power cameras at the edge.
history: Kneron was founded in 2015 to bring tiny on-device AI to IoT, developing an AI-in-sensor architecture for low-power cameras. The company raised $48.7M in 2022 from investors including Foxconn and shipped successive KL-series edge NPUs. It continues expanding into on-device large-language-model applications and automotive vision partnerships across the US and Asia, aiming at battery-powered devices.

name: Horizon Robotics
short_description: Shanghai/HK-listed maker of automotive ADAS and robotics SoCs.
why_relevant: Mass ADAS adoption in Chinese EVs at software-defined scale.
history: Horizon Robotics was founded in 2015 by former Baidu executive Yu Kai to build automotive ADAS and robotics processors. The company's Journey and Matrix SoC families became standard in Chinese electric vehicles, and it listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange in late 2024. Horizon now operates as a profitable, public supplier of software-defined driving platforms driving mass ADAS adoption in China.

name: Black Sesame Technologies
short_description: Hong Kong-listed designer of automotive-grade AI chips.
why_relevant: Racing toward L3 autonomous compute in China's EV fleets.
history: Black Sesame Technologies was founded in 2016 to design automotive-grade AI chips, launching its Huashan autonomous driving SoCs. The company attracted strategic backing from Xiaomi and others and listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange in 2024. It continues developing L3-oriented computing platforms for Chinese EV fleets racing toward autonomous driving, expanding its customer base among domestic automakers.

name: Enflame
short_description: Chinese AI chip company scaling data-center accelerators.
why_relevant: One of the domestic GPU-equivalent options in the Chinese AI buildout.
history: Enflame was founded in 2018 to build Chinese data-center AI accelerators, developing its Suoyuan NPU line for training and inference. The company raised hundreds of millions of dollars across several rounds and achieved volume deployments inside China's digital infrastructure. It positions its accelerators and software stack as domestic options in China's effort to reduce reliance on imported GPUs, benefiting from the state-backed AI buildout.

name: Cambricon
short_description: First Chinese AI chip IP public listing, now designing acceleration cards.
why_relevant: Early mover on cloud AI chips, listed on the STAR market.
history: Cambricon was founded in 2016 by Chen Tianshi and became China's first AI-chip IP company to hold a public listing. The company listed on the STAR Market in 2020 and expanded from processor IP into its MLU accelerator product line for cloud AI. It remains a flagship vehicle in China's domestic silicon strategy, supplying acceleration cards and terminals across the country's AI infrastructure.

name: Biren Technology
short_description: Develops general-purpose GPUs for server AI training.
why_relevant: Attempts a full-stack CUDA-class offering for the Chinese market.
history: Biren Technology was founded in 2021 to develop general-purpose GPUs for AI training in China, announcing its BR100 series and ambitions for a full CUDA-class stack. The company raised large rounds from state-linked funds, reaching a multi-billion-dollar valuation. It continues building training-oriented GPUs and a software ecosystem to serve as a domestic alternative to imported accelerators.

name: Achronix
short_description: Speedster eFPGA and AI/ML FPGA IP for high-speed acceleration.
why_relevant: Embedded FPGA cores keep programmable logic near the data.
history: Achronix was founded in 2004 to push FPGA performance, delivering its Speedster high-speed FPGAs and pioneering embedded FPGA IP with Speedcore. The company went public via a SPAC combination in 2021 and expanded its Speedster7t AI acceleration fabric. It now licenses eFPGA cores and sells standalone FPGAs for networking, AI and data-center acceleration workloads, keeping programmable logic close to the data that needs it.

name: Flex Logix
short_description: Pioneers embedded programmable fabric licensed into other silicon.
why_relevant: Sells flexible logic that chips can reprogram after shipping.
history: Flex Logix was founded in 2014 to commercialize embedded FPGA fabric, licensing its EFLX architecture across semiconductor platforms. The company built an edge inference accelerator line and delivered eFPGA IP to a range of chipmakers, and in 2025 announced it would wind down operations after years in the market. Its technology nevertheless demonstrated the broad viability of reprogrammable logic embedded in other silicon.

name: Astera Labs
short_description: Data-center connectivity chips easing PCIe and CXL scaling.
why_relevant: IPO'd as the connectivity layer of the AI data-center buildout.
history: Astera Labs was founded in 2017 by Jitendra Mohan to build connectivity silicon for PCIe and CXL in AI servers. The company strengthened its position with Aries retimers and the Leo, Taurus and Scorpio product families, and went public on Nasdaq in March 2024 in a well-received IPO. It now serves nearly every major AI platform vendor, cementing its role as the connectivity layer of the AI data-center buildout.

name: Credo Technology
short_description: High-speed SerDes and cabling that connect AI clusters at scale.
why_relevant: Tie insides of AI racks across thousands of GPUs with clean copper.
history: Credo Technology was founded in 2007 to advance high-speed SerDes technology and interconnection for the AI era. The company listed on Nasdaq in January 2022 and expanded its HiWire active electrical cables into high-volume deployments linking thousands of GPUs. Its AEC product family has become an important way to connect AI clusters at scale while avoiding the cost of optical interconnect.
